My personal hypothesis is that security is impossible as long as we keep using Von Neumann architecture in our computers.

Von Neuman architecture means data and instructions are stored on the same memory and it is up to the software to figure out which is which. So any data can be executed as code with malicious intent. The most fundamental flaw of the computers today is the architecture itself. Von Neumann probably knew that from the beginning. He was involved with Ultra, he was Turing's counterpart in America and knew everything about theory of keeping secrets. He was one of the first people that actually understood Turing's machine. I think this fundamental flaw was one of the reason computer became declassified at all, otherwise they may have been kept secret to this day.

We have reasonable chance of improvement with the Harvard architecture. In that model data and instructions are kept separate. This is architecturally much more difficult to exploit.

A further improvement is possible if we add a third kind of memory specifically for keeping secrets. This memory should not be directly accessible to the CPU but only queryable trough a separate crypto processor. Somewhat like the architecture of the smartcards.
